name: Libertarian conservatism
summary: Libertarian conservatism pursues conservative ends, such as moral order, religion and constitutional government, through liberty and free markets rather than through state power. It favors minimal government, free-market capitalism with privatization and often Austrian-school monetary views, and treats economic freedom as bound up with political freedom. It is mostly American, and the tension between liberty and virtue is its recurring fault line.
scope: The 'conservatarian' strand the defining sources describe: American right-wing people who, in Charles C.W. Cooke's words, feel conservative around libertarians and libertarian around conservatives (Reason, The Week, Carolina Journal). They split from libertarians on immigration, foreign policy and sometimes abortion, and from traditional conservatives on federalism, same-sex marriage and drugs (Reason interview), and The American Conservative traces the idea to the Buckley and Frank Meyer fusion of traditional ends with free means. It excludes anarcho-capitalist paleolibertarianism and traditionalist conservatism that wants the state to enforce virtue.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Cooke does not support the libertarian solution of privatizing marriage and disagrees with libertarians who say the state has no business conferring special status on relationships.

abortion-legal.rationale: Conservatarians side mostly with conservatives on abortion; Cooke argues that a life is a life and that anyone interested in individual liberty must protect the innocent, and defends restrictions on access to abortion.

central-planning.rationale: Cooke cites Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' to question whether things can be run well from the center, arguing decisions must be left to those familiar with specific circumstances.

decide-locally.rationale: Cooke's central proposal is a return to federalism: the federal government should leave a good number of questions to states and localities so that people can live as they see fit ('If you don't like the way people live in Mississippi, live somewhere else').

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Cooke wants the right to defend the Constitution as written, changing it through the Article V amendment process, and says protections of fundamental rights are best secured at the national level, not left to local politics.

experts-over-public.rationale: Cooke rejects the progressive belief that an educated, well-staffed central authority can determine how citizens should live, citing Hayek on why decisions belong with people who know the local circumstances.

foreign-policy-non-interference.rationale: Cooke calls himself a firm believer in American world leadership and finds skepticism stretching into all-out disengagement worrying, though America can lead without rushing to every fire; the reviewers describe his foreign policy as interventionist.

free-trade.rationale: Cooke's indictment of the Bush-era Republicans lists that they undermined free trade, treating free trade as a principle the right abandoned.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Cooke endorses the libertarian view that the war on drugs failed, groups conservatarians with libertarians on drug legalization, and wants the federal government out of the field and policy left to the states; the reviewers note he doesn't say whether this covers every drug.

limit-guns.rationale: Cooke is a serious opponent of gun control and holds up the right's gun-debate victories as the model of success.

military-superiority.rationale: Cooke defends military spending and American world leadership, and says the US cannot give up its position without letting another nation take that role, which he does not want.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Cooke rejects the libertarian view that the state has no business recognizing marriage, saying society has a residual interest in how the next generation is reared, and he does not support privatizing marriage; this goes beyond protection from physical violence.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Cooke faults the Republicans for favoring the interests of big business over a free market.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Conservatarians side with conservatives on immigration; Cooke favors tough border enforcement and limits on immigration, and says the existing polity sets the criteria for new arrivals.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Cooke's federalism rests on the point that the states created the federal government, not the other way around, which doesn't fit a national legislature able to take back any power it gave regions.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Conservatarians side with libertarians on gay marriage; Cooke argues conservatives should accept it because suppressing a change that arose organically does little good, while holding there is no constitutional right to it and leaving the details to the states.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Cooke opposes gun control and defends ready access to firearms, so he rejects barring people outside state forces from having weapons.

state-harmful.rationale: Cooke wants the federal government to keep performing the basic functions smaller entities cannot, such as national defense and border security, in a Founding-era framework.

notes: The defining sources are journalism and reviews of Charles C.W. Cooke's The Conservatarian Manifesto, so answers rest on the positions they report him taking; the group is split with libertarians on immigration, foreign policy and abortion, and with traditional conservatives on federalism, gay marriage and drugs. Reviewers note the book gives little attention to economics and religion, so those statements are null.
